feedback.reason: The provider exceeds the request SLA, so the contract needs a bounded call deadline, one attempt owner, and local isolation. Jitter spreads eligible retries without multiplying them across layers.
feedback.details: Set an outbound deadline shorter than 700 ms and make one layer own a maximum of three attempts with jittered backoff for transient failures only. Bound in-flight requests for this provider and report terminal/deferred outcomes. Do not retry validation/auth failures, and do not couple other providers to its breaker. This contains both waiting and retry amplification.

messages.text: Independent retry loops multiply attempts and can exceed both the caller SLA and provider capacity.
The provider is slower than the 700 ms budget, so an unbounded wait consumes shared request capacity.
Permanent errors will not recover through retry and waste the bounded provider capacity.
A provider-specific failure would block unrelated healthy dependencies.

options.text: Use one retry owner with a bounded attempt budget and provider deadline; release the caller slot at its SLA.
Let the SDK, gateway, and delivery worker each retry three times whenever the provider misses its deadline.
Wait indefinitely for the provider and hold the gateway request worker until it returns.
Retry timeouts, validation errors, and authentication failures identically until an attempt succeeds.
Use one shared circuit breaker for all providers so repeated timeouts here stop calls to healthy providers.

prompt: A notification provider has a 700 ms caller SLA and usually responds in 1.5 seconds. Only one layer may retry, with at most three attempts and jittered backoff; other providers must keep serving requests. What timeout/retry contract fits?

feedback.reason: The write may already be committed when its response is lost. A stable identity bound to actor and payload makes the retry return that same append rather than duplicate or alter attribution.
feedback.details: Persist the operation ID with the immutable payload and authenticated principal in the ledger’s idempotency boundary. A retry with matching parameters returns the original result; a changed actor or event body under A17 is a conflict. The caller may stop waiting, but timeout is not a command to undo the commit. Dedup state must survive process replacement.

messages.text: A new ID describes a second append and can duplicate the same administrator action.
The database already committed the event; a network timeout does not roll back that durable write.
The same operation identity must not let a retry change or forge the actor attribution.
A process restart erases the dedup record even though the durable ledger entry remains.

options.text: Retry the append with the same operation ID and return the already committed event on replay.
Retry using a fresh event ID so the ledger can distinguish the second request from the first.
Treat the lost response as proof the append did not commit and delete any record matching A17 before retrying.
Reuse A17 but accept the actor name from the retry payload without checking it against authentication.
Remember A17 only in the API process memory and append again after that process restarts.

prompt: An administrator appends an audit event using operation ID A17. The database commits it, but the response is lost; the client retries the same action. The record must appear once and retain actor attribution. What retry contract is required?

feedback.reason: Retry identity handles delivery ambiguity; the revision guard handles ordering between different updates. Preserve both through retry so a late 41 cannot overwrite 42.
feedback.details: Retry only eligible transient failures with the original event ID and source revision. At the shipment owner, compare the incoming revision in the same transaction as the state write. A duplicate ID is a no-op; a lower revision is rejected/quarantined; a higher revision advances state. Never convert a stale conflict into an unconditional retry.

messages.text: A retry becomes indistinguishable from a new update and may bypass dedup or monotonic order.
Delayed revision 41 can arrive after 42 and overwrite newer shipment state.
A stale revision conflict is not transient; removing the precondition causes state regression.
The receiver may not have accepted a transiently delayed event; same-ID retries are safe when receiver dedup and revision checks exist.

options.text: Retry the same event identity and apply only revisions newer than the shipment’s current revision.
Assign a new event ID and reset the revision whenever a delivery times out.
Apply whichever authenticated carrier message arrives last, regardless of its revision.
Retry a conditional-write conflict by dropping the revision precondition and writing the payload.
Drop the update after the first timeout because retries may be duplicated.

prompt: A carrier update with shipment revision 42 times out at the receiver and is retried later; a revision 41 event is also delayed in transit. What retry rule keeps the shipment from regressing?

feedback.reason: The provider may have accepted work before the deadline. Durable identity and reconciliation preserve one billable intent while its result is unknown; the retry budget belongs to one owner.
feedback.details: Persist the intent and provider idempotency key before dispatch. On timeout, report pending/unknown and query or reconcile the same provider operation. Retry only transiently eligible calls under one bounded owner and the same identity. Do not create a new job ID until the prior intent is conclusively resolved as not executed or a new user intent is submitted.

messages.text: The first provider job may already be running, so a fresh identity can create a second charge.
The timeout records loss of a response, not proof the provider did no work.
Unbounded retries amplify load and can repeat billable attempts if the provider lacks perfect dedup.
Unknown is actionable only when the system can query and resolve the original intent.

options.text: Reconcile the existing extraction operation after timeout; do not create a second billable job.
Start a new provider job ID whenever the worker deadline expires.
Mark the job failed at the deadline and tell the client to submit a new extraction.
Retry the provider indefinitely at every worker and client timeout with no shared budget.
Return a generic unknown response but keep no durable operation record to reconcile later.

prompt: An extraction worker times out after the billable provider may have started the job. The client may retry, but the provider outcome can remain unknown for several minutes. What deadline/retry contract avoids duplicate billing?

feedback.reason: A deadline cannot decide the inventory result. Exposing pending/unknown under the original operation identity lets the service reconcile without turning an uncertain first claim into another allocation.
feedback.details: Persist the allocation intent before calling inventory. If the response is lost, retain its stable identity and report pending/unknown. Query the same operation or reconcile with the inventory owner; only a confirmed no-claim result can become final failure. Bound retries and status polling. Do not use a new identity solely because the caller timed out.

messages.text: The first claim may already have committed, so a new ID can reserve a second seat.
A probable outcome is not an authoritative reservation and may falsely confirm an unallocated ticket.
Repeated allocation attempts can compete for or consume multiple seats.
The caller cannot safely tell whether to wait, retry, or contact support when the state is discarded.

options.text: Query the same allocation intent after deadline and keep UNKNOWN until the inventory owner resolves it.
Return failed and instruct the client to retry with a new allocation ID.
Return confirmed whenever the inventory call times out because the seat probably committed.
Repeat allocation at every poll until a success response arrives, without checking the original intent state.
Return only a generic server error and discard the request identity so no status can resolve later.

prompt: A ticket reservation deadline expires after the inventory authority may have claimed a seat. The client must not allocate another seat while the result is uncertain. What response and retry policy is correct?

feedback.reason: Deadline and cancellation control work lifetime, while tenant authorization is a non-negotiable query boundary. Propagate cancellation without changing the scope predicate.
feedback.details: Derive the tenant from authenticated identity and authorize the case before starting the query. Carry the deadline/cancel signal into database operations and stop work when canceled; ignore late results. If the deadline is exceeded, return a timeout/unavailable outcome scoped to that request. Never broaden a query to meet latency or move tenant filtering to the client.

messages.text: Meeting latency cannot justify crossing tenant scope; an unscoped query exposes protected data.
Uncanceled backend work continues consuming capacity after the caller no longer needs it.
Other tenant data is already disclosed and the authorization decision belongs at the server.
A canceled request is not a transient provider failure; an automatic fresh query defeats cancellation and can amplify load.

options.text: Propagate cancellation to the tenant-authorized query and stop work at its 300 ms deadline.
If authorization is slow, run the search without the tenant predicate so the 300 ms deadline is met.
Let canceled searches run to completion in the shared worker pool and return results if they eventually finish.
Return a broad result set before the deadline and rely on the client to hide other tenants’ rows.
Treat cancellation as a query failure and immediately start a fresh unbounded search under a new request identity.

prompt: A tenant-scoped support search has a 300 ms deadline and supports cancellation. Cancellation must stop expensive query work, but it must never skip tenant authorization or return another tenant’s results. What deadline/cancellation contract fits?

feedback.reason: Retry depends on outcome class: temporary dependency errors may retry within budget, while not-found and stale states are semantically distinct. A deadline bounds the read even during source outage.
feedback.details: Use a finite request deadline. Return metadata with its age when within the 20-second policy; return stale/not-yet-indexed if the projection exceeds it, confirmed 404 only when source absence is known, and 503 when the source cannot answer. Retry only transient failures with a bounded attempt policy. Never turn a dependency outage into absence or retry a permanent 404 forever.

messages.text: A confirmed absent asset is not a transient failure, and unlimited retries consume capacity without changing the result.
The caller cannot rely on the stated freshness bound if stale age is hidden.
Unavailable source state does not prove the asset is absent.
The read has no completion bound and can occupy resources during a two-minute outage.

options.text: Retry only explicitly transient source failures; preserve stale, confirmed missing, and unavailable as distinct outcomes.
Retry every not-found response indefinitely until an asset appears.
Serve any cached value as fresh success even when its age exceeds 20 seconds.
Return 404 whenever the source is unreachable so clients can stop retrying.
Wait indefinitely for the source to recover before returning metadata or an error.

prompt: A metadata projection can return data up to 20 seconds stale. A source outage may last 2 minutes, and retrying a 404 cannot repair it. What deadline and retry policy should a metadata read use?

feedback.reason: A timeout creates an unknown physical outcome. Preserve the same command identity and let the actuation owner deduplicate; stopping the caller wait is not cancellation of the accepted command.
feedback.details: Use one operation identity from acceptance through every delivery and device retry. The device records the identity at the physical effect boundary and returns the prior result for a replay. If actuation may have occurred without a recorded response, report unknown and reconcile rather than issuing a fresh command. Bound delivery attempts and distinguish cancel-wait from an explicit command-cancel operation.

messages.text: The prior command may already have executed; a new identity can repeat the unsafe effect.
The cancellation only ends the caller’s wait; delivery or actuation may already have occurred.
The gateway may not know whether the device acted before a response was lost; dedup belongs at the effect boundary too.
Repeated delivery can actuate multiple times, while unbounded attempts overload an offline device path.

options.text: Cancel the caller’s wait without canceling a possibly delivered command; retry with the same device sequence ID.
Create a new command ID after every timeout so the device can retry the physical action.
Treat client cancellation as proof that the device never received or executed the command.
Deduplicate sends at the gateway and assume the device cannot execute a repeated delivery.
Redeliver continuously until the device responds, without a stable identity or bounded retry budget.

prompt: An IoT command request times out after delivery may have reached the device. Canceling the client’s wait must not imply the physical action did not occur. What retry contract prevents repeating the unsafe command?

feedback.reason: At-least-once delivery requires stable identity and receiver dedup. One bounded retry owner with backoff avoids retry amplification while keeping accepted events recoverable.
feedback.details: Persist the event and delivery state at the sender, retry the same event ID with exponential backoff under one owner, and stop at a declared attempt/time budget with observable dead-letter state. The receiver records the ID and effect intent durably before returning acknowledgment. A timeout remains ambiguous, so a retry is the same event, not a new one.

messages.text: A new ID defeats deduplication and makes retries appear as separate logical events.
Two retry owners can multiply deliveries and overwhelm a recovering receiver.
No backoff or terminal limit creates unbounded load during an outage.
A crash after acknowledgment can lose the event while the sender believes delivery completed.

options.text: Let one sender own bounded retries and let the receiver deduplicate the stable delivery ID.
Generate a fresh event ID on each timeout so every attempt is distinguishable at the receiver.
Let both the sender and receiver retry each other without coordinating attempt counts.
Retry immediately and forever until an HTTP success is observed.
Have the receiver acknowledge after parsing, before its dedup record or side effect is durable.

prompt: A webhook sender receives no acknowledgment before its deadline. Delivery is at-least-once; the receiver deduplicates by event ID. Only one component may own retries, with exponential backoff and a maximum attempt window. What policy should be used?

feedback.reason: Transient network failure and a stale revision are different outcomes. Preserve the precondition for bounded transient retries and return conflicts for explicit merge.
feedback.details: A retry keeps the same expected revision and operation identity. Retry only transient transport/service failures within the two-attempt budget and one owner. A 412/conflict is not retried as an unconditional write; the client reloads or merges and submits a new intentional edit against the new revision. This prevents late retries from overwriting another collaborator.

messages.text: Removing the precondition converts a detected stale edit into a silent lost update.
Conflicts require a user merge decision; endless attempts cannot make stale content current.
A guessed revision may still be stale and can misrepresent the user’s intended base.
Layered budgets can exceed the intended two attempts and amplify write contention.

options.text: Retry a transient write only with the original expected revision; surface conflicts for a fresh read.
After a conflict, retry without If-Match so the user’s edit eventually overwrites the current document.
Retry conflicts, timeouts, and validation errors indefinitely until the write succeeds.
Guess the latest revision from a cache and resend the edit using that value without re-reading the document.
Let both the editor and gateway each perform two retries independently.

prompt: Two collaborators edit revision 28. A stale write returns a version conflict; a network timeout may be transient. The client may retry at most twice, and must never turn a stale edit into an unconditional overwrite. What retry contract fits?

feedback.reason: Stable IDs make each request retry-safe, but the shared stock invariant spans distinct buyer intents. The authoritative atomic claim is still required.
feedback.details: Persist each intent ID so a retry resolves the same reservation, then atomically decrement/claim stock at the inventory owner. Only one transaction can consume the last unit; the other receives conflict or unavailable. Idempotency and deadlines address per-intent repetition and waiting, not cross-intent concurrency.

messages.text: The keys prevent duplicate execution of each intent, not competition between two distinct intents.
A new key may repeat a claim and creates an additional operation instead of resolving the original.
Both distinct requests can read one unit before either transaction commits.
A time budget limits waiting; it does not make the stock mutation atomic.

options.text: Retry each stable reserve intent, but enforce stock availability atomically across distinct buyers.
Assume per-request idempotency keys alone prevent two different buyers from claiming the last unit.
Assign a new key on timeout and retry until each buyer gets a success response.
Read the remaining count before each retry and reserve if it is positive.
Use a short retry deadline as the concurrency control and accept both results if they return before expiration.

prompt: One unit remains in stock. Two distinct reserve intents time out and retry safely by their own IDs. The system must not sell two units or confirm both requests. Which retry boundary is needed?

feedback.reason: The same learner intent can be delivered more than once. Stable identity and set-state semantics make retries converge, while one bounded owner prevents attempt multiplication.
feedback.details: Persist the submission ID and learner/module binding with the completion result. Retry only transient failures under the progress service’s two-attempt budget, reusing that identity; a duplicate returns the recorded state. Do not increment on each attempt or allow another layer to create extra retries. A lost response is not evidence that no completion was stored.

messages.text: The progress counter changes before the response, so ignoring a duplicate response does not undo duplicate increments.
Multiple owners can create more than two attempts and duplicate completion state.
Each identity appears to be a new completion and defeats deduplication of the original intent.
Without durable state, the service cannot know whether to repeat or report the prior result.

options.text: Let one service own at most two retries of the idempotent completion set operation.
Send incrementCompletion on every attempt and let the client ignore duplicate response messages.
Let the SDK and progress service each retry twice with independent identities.
Use a new submission ID on retry so each attempt can be audited independently.
Retry a timeout but keep no record of whether the original completion committed.

prompt: A learner submission marks a module complete. The response can be lost, and only the progress service may retry, at most twice. Repeating the same completion must not add progress twice. What retry rule should apply?

feedback.reason: The retry policy must preserve revision order. Retry only eligible transient failures under one bounded owner; a stale revision is a conflict, never an unconditional retry.
feedback.details: Bind the operation identity and revision to the publish request. The price authority applies a conditional monotonic update, and checkout validates the committed revision. Retry transient storage failures at most twice with the same identity. If current revision is already 52, reject stale 51 and report conflict. Cache invalidation can follow but is not publication success.

messages.text: A stale revision conflict is permanent for that payload; unconditional retry would roll the price back from 52.
Independent retry owners exceed the budget and can reorder updates.
The write may have committed before the response was lost; a fresh identity can reapply stale data.
Checkout may still observe the previous revision despite the success response.

options.text: Retry transient publish failures under the same revision precondition; never turn a stale revision into an unconditional write.
On any failure, retry revision 51 as an unconditional overwrite so it can eventually publish.
Let the merchant client and gateway each retry twice with separate revision identities.
Treat a timeout for revision 51 as proof it did not commit, then publish it under a new key.
Return success when an invalidation event is queued, before the conditional price update commits.

prompt: A merchant publishes price revision 52. An earlier revision 51 update may be retried after a timeout; retry attempts are limited to two and only transient storage failures are retryable. What deadline/retry contract keeps checkout from seeing an obsolete price?

feedback.reason: A gateway timeout leaves enforcement unknown. The operation must remain pending until the authorization boundary confirms old sessions are rejected; a success response cannot precede that guarantee.
feedback.details: Use a stable revocation operation and track the epoch/status observed by each relevant enforcement path. During lag or timeout, return pending/unknown and fail closed where current revocation state cannot be verified. Query or retry that same operation; do not allow old sessions because the response was lost. Success means enforcement, not merely queue acceptance.

messages.text: The timeout does not prove enforcement; old sessions may remain authorized after a false success.
A revocation may have committed even though its response was lost, and fail-open behavior preserves risk.
Multiple identities complicate ordering and still do not prove all authorization nodes enforce the revocation.
Unobserved propagation cannot support a success claim or a fail-closed authorization decision.

options.text: Keep revocation pending until every relevant authorization boundary enforces it; do not report success on timeout.
Return success when the gateway times out so callers stop retrying and assume the old sessions are invalid.
Treat the timeout as proof nothing changed and continue allowing old sessions until a new request arrives.
Create a new revocation operation each time the caller times out and allow nodes to process them independently.
Queue invalidation and provide no status or enforcement watermark, while continuing to accept sessions during lag.

prompt: Credential revocation returns after a gateway timeout, and some authorization nodes may still accept old sessions. The operation is security-sensitive and must fail closed. What should callers observe and what retry is safe?

feedback.reason: The worker job lifecycle is longer than the client wait. Keep accepted state durable, recover workers under a finite policy, and decouple canceling a poll from canceling the job.
feedback.details: Persist job J8 and its input identity before acceptance. Worker leases allow a replacement to resume after failure; bound retries and record terminal failure when recovery is exhausted. A canceled status request only stops that response path. An explicit job-cancel command can change work state separately, with its own race and result semantics.

messages.text: The caller canceled waiting, not the already accepted transcoding operation.
Unbounded recovery can consume resources indefinitely and gives no observable final outcome.
Polling does not create a new intent; another ID can duplicate the same expensive work.
A request deadline measures waiting time and says nothing about job completion.

options.text: Cancel status polling independently; the durably accepted worker job continues under its own retry policy.
Propagate cancellation of the status poll directly to the worker and delete job J8.
Retry failed transcoding forever with no lease, attempt budget, or terminal status.
Create a new job ID whenever a status poll times out or is canceled.
Mark J8 complete when its request deadline ends even if the worker has not produced an artifact.

prompt: A transcode job is durably accepted under jobId J8. The caller’s status poll is canceled at 250 ms, while the worker may run for 25 minutes and can be replaced. What deadline/retry rule preserves the accepted work?

feedback.reason: A rule read may time out, but timeout does not authorize repeating a schema mutation or claiming rollback. Bounded reads and explicit rollback state preserve safety.
feedback.details: Set a 100 ms deadline for rule evaluation and return an explicit unavailable outcome if it cannot complete. Keep persisted records readable by old clients independently of the flag. Track rollback as a durable state transition with an observable completion result. Retry an idempotent read within budget if allowed; reconcile an unknown migration outcome before any further write.

messages.text: An ambiguous timeout can repeat an irreversible or non-idempotent migration and break rollback.
Changing the flag does not restore incompatible persisted records.
The required read budget is violated, and waiting does not provide a safe outcome.
Operators and callers cannot tell if the rollout is still active or safely rolled back.

options.text: Return an explicit rollback result within deadline and keep persisted data readable by both versions.
Retry the schema mutation after every timeout until it reports success, without checking whether the first attempt committed.
Return rollback success when the flag write is accepted, even though old readers may no longer read persisted data.
Wait beyond the 100 ms deadline until the rule service responds and keep the request open.
Return a generic error on timeout without recording whether rollback is pending or completed.

prompt: A rollout rule read has a 100 ms deadline. Disabling the feature must produce an explicit rollback result, while persisted records remain readable by old clients. A timeout must not blindly repeat an irreversible schema migration. What retry contract fits?

feedback.reason: Retries need stable identity, while the overlap rule spans distinct intents. A timeout remains pending/unknown until reconciled; atomic reservation guards each commit.
feedback.details: Keep the same operation ID through each caller retry and resolve it to the recorded attempt. A timeout does not cancel or fail the reservation. At the resource owner, commit only if no conflicting interval exists in the same atomic transaction. Return conflict to the losing intent and confirm only after commit. The retry budget controls attempts, not the invariant.

messages.text: The keys identify different intents and do not enforce the shared resource’s no-overlap invariant.
A retry becomes another reservation attempt and can duplicate or obscure the original result.
The original write may have committed before its response was lost; timeout is an unknown outcome.
Concurrent requests can pass separate reads; only the atomic final write protects the invariant.

options.text: Resolve timeout through the same booking intent and atomic overlap guard; do not confirm an unknown result.
Assume distinct idempotency keys make overlapping requests safe and confirm both when their retries succeed.
Generate a new booking ID for each retry so the service can attempt the slot again.
Treat a caller timeout as proof the original reservation did not commit, then release the slot and accept another booking.
Read availability before every retry and confirm if the range looks free.

prompt: Two booking requests for overlapping ranges on the same resource have distinct idempotency keys. One response times out, and each caller may retry twice. What deadline/retry contract preserves no-overlap and avoids duplicate confirmation?
